PAPER: Original Article JHSMR Journal of Health Science and Medical Research The Modulatory Effects of Pinocembrin from the Nigerian Propolis on IL-6, IL-1β, and Adipokines in Rats with Chronic Glucose and Fructose Administration Mustafa Ibrahim Oladayo, Ph.D. Department of Physiology, Faculty of Basic Medical Science, Federal University Oye-Ekiti, Ekiti 371101, Nigeria. Received 15 January 2025 l Accepted 17 February 2025 l Published online 10 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: The study investigated the effects of pinocembrin on cytokines and the adipokines associated with metabolic disturbances that arise from prolonged sugar intake. Material and Methods: Twenty-four male Wistar rats were divided into 4 groups: control, glucose/fructose administration, glucose/fructose administration plus pinocembrin treatment, and glucose/fructose administration plus metformin treatment. The control group was administered distilled water orally, while the glucose/fructose group received an oral sugar solution comprising 30% glucose and 20% fructose. The pinocembrin and metformin treatment groups were given the same sugar solution, but received either pinocembrin or metformin as an additional component, respectively. Administration continued for 8 weeks, after which blood samples were collected for biochemical analysis. Results: Chronic administration of glucose and fructose led to the dysregulation of adipokines and inflammatory markers, hyperinsulinemia and hyperglycaemia. However, treatment with pinocembrin significantly mitigated these metabolic and inflammatory alterations. Conclusion: The findings suggest that the prophylactic use of pinocembrin from the Nigerian propolis has the potential to modulate glucose and lipid metabolism, as well as inflammatory pathways, thereby preventing sugar-induced metabolic disturbances. JSON: Name: pinocembrin_sugar_metabolic_modulation Title: Prophylactic oral administration of pinocembrin to prevent sugar-induced hyperglycaemia, insulin resistance, inflammatory cytokine elevation and adipokine dysregulation in a rat model Short Hypothesis: Daily oral administration of pinocembrin (50 mg/kg) during chronic co-administration of glucose and fructose prevents increases in plasma IL-6, IL-1β, fasting glucose, fasting insulin (HOMA-IR) and leptin, and prevents decreases in adiponectin, compared with untreated sugar-fed rats. Related Work: Previous work has established that chronic high-sugar (glucose/fructose) diets in rodents induce hyperglycaemia, hyperinsulinaemia, insulin resistance and a pro-inflammatory state characterized by increased IL-6 and IL-1β and disrupted adipokines (increased leptin, decreased adiponectin). Propolis extracts and the flavanone pinocembrin have been reported to exhibit anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and metabolic regulatory properties in in vitro and small-animal studies, and metformin is commonly used as a pharmacologic positive control for metabolic protection. Existing studies are limited by heterogeneous propolis composition, use of crude extracts rather than purified pinocembrin, small group sizes, incomplete dose–response characterization, limited mechanistic interrogation of signalling pathways (for example NF-κB and Nrf2), short treatment windows, and scarce pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic data, which together constrain reproducibility and translational interpretation. Abstract: Chronic excessive intake of glucose and fructose produces insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia and low-grade inflammation mediated by cytokines and adipokines. This project evaluates whether prophylactic oral administration of purified pinocembrin prevents sugar-induced metabolic and inflammatory disturbances in a rodent model. Using a controlled experimental design, pinocembrin will be administered concurrently with a defined glucose/fructose drinking solution and outcomes will include fasting glucose, fasting insulin and HOMA-IR, plasma IL-6 and IL-1β, leptin and adiponectin, oral glucose tolerance and tissue markers of inflammatory signalling. The main contribution is a rigorous, dose-aware preclinical pipeline that tests prophylactic efficacy of a defined natural product compound, compares it to a pharmacologic comparator, and links systemic readouts to tissue-level signalling and pharmacokinetics. Expected outcomes are demonstration of preventive efficacy of pinocembrin on metabolic and inflammatory endpoints and identification of candidate molecular pathways for subsequent mechanistic and translational studies. Experiments: Experimental design: male Wistar rats, randomized, n=10 per group. Groups: (A) control (vehicle water); (B) sugar (30% glucose + 20% fructose in drinking water); (C) sugar + pinocembrin 25 mg/kg/day oral; (D) sugar + pinocembrin 50 mg/kg/day oral; (E) sugar + pinocembrin 100 mg/kg/day oral; (F) sugar + metformin 50 mg/kg/day oral (positive control); (G) sugar + pinocembrin 50 mg/kg/day + NF-κB activator (low-dose LPS challenge for mechanistic ablation); (H) therapeutic arm: sugar for 4 weeks then pinocembrin 50 mg/kg/day from weeks 5–8. Duration: 8 weeks for prophylactic arms, 8 weeks total for therapeutic arm. Assays and endpoints: primary endpoints — fasting plasma glucose (glucometer, mg/dL), fasting insulin (ELISA, μU/mL), HOMA-IR calculation; inflammatory cytokines — plasma IL-6 and IL-1β (ELISA, pg/mL); adipokines — plasma leptin and adiponectin (ELISA, ng/mL); secondary endpoints — oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT, area under curve), insulin tolerance test (ITT, KITT), liver and epididymal white adipose tissue histology (H&E, adipocyte size, NAS scoring), tissue protein expression of NF-κB p65, p-IκBα, Nrf2 and downstream targets (Western blot, densitometry), tissue mRNA levels of inflammatory markers (qPCR), plasma lipid panel (TG, LDL, HDL), liver enzymes (ALT/AST), and pinocembrin plasma and tissue concentrations (HPLC-MS). Baselines and controls: group A and B as negative and disease baselines; group F (metformin) as pharmacologic comparator. Ablation/comparison studies: dose–response (25/50/100 mg/kg), therapeutic vs prophylactic start, and NF-κB activation co-treatment to test dependency on NF-κB signalling. Sample size justification: powered to detect a 20% difference in IL-6 with alpha=0.05 and power=0.8 (~n=8–10). Statistical analysis: one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc for endpoint comparisons, repeated-measures ANOVA for longitudinal measures (body weight, OGTT), effect sizes (Cohen's d), significance threshold p<0.05. Pre-specified comparisons: (B vs A), (C–E vs B), (F vs B), dose trend test across C–E, (G vs D) to test mechanistic ablation, and (therapeutic arm vs B) to test reversal versus prevention. Risk Factors and Limitations: Model and generalizability: rodent glucose/fructose co-administration models replicate features of human metabolic dysregulation but do not fully represent human diet heterogeneity, sex differences (male-only cohort limits inference to females), or long-term comorbidities. Compound variability and formulation: natural-source variability of propolis requires strict purification and batch characterization; oral bioavailability, first-pass metabolism and active metabolites of pinocembrin may differ between rats and humans. Mechanistic ambiguity: observed systemic effects may be pleiotropic and not exclusively mediated by NF-κB or Nrf2 pathways; pharmacologic modulators may have off-target effects. Sample size and statistical power: effect sizes smaller than anticipated may lead to false negatives. Safety and toxicity: chronic dosing may reveal organ toxicity or off-target effects not predicted by short studies. Assay and measurement biases: ELISA kit cross-reactivity, inter-assay variability and single-timepoint sampling can bias estimates. Ethical and regulatory constraints: limits on invasive sampling and on translation of doses from rodents to humans. Scalability: large-scale or chronic studies to support clinical translation will require additional PK/PD, GMP-grade compound production, and regulatory toxicology data.
